item.title: San Francisco Isn’t Giving Up on Turning More of Its Offices Into Homes
item.description:
In the years after the pandemic, many city officials and developers saw an opportunity to turn unused offices into apartments. San Francisco, with roughly a third of its 100 million square feet of office space vacant, had the potential to be a nucleus for office-to-residential activity.

But as cities like New York, Washington and Chicago began offering tax incentives for conversions, San Francisco did not offer similar programs for builders. And since then, San Francisco has yet to see a single office conversion even as thousands of projects are underway and being completed in other cities.

The city is now is trying to change that. This year, officials adopted a law that allows developers to get back a portion of their future property taxes, over 30 years, on commercial buildings converted to new housing.

The financial reimbursement is available for projects downtown, which includes the Financial District, South of Market area and Civic Center neighborhood, and is meant to help alleviate the financial risk of conversions.

So far, three developers have submitted projects for the program.

“We’ve got about 30 million square feet of vacant space, so we knew we had a significant problem to tackle,” said Anne Taupier, executive director of the city’s Office of Economic and Workforce Development.

City officials are hoping the new tax incentive will fuel conversions the way tax abatement programs have in New York and Washington. Those are the top two markets for office conversions, with nearly 25,000 units in development combined as of the start of this year, according to RentCafe, an apartment search platform and research firm.

In 2023, a study by a group of public policy, planning and architecture firms determined that many office buildings in San Francisco were suitable for conversion because of factors like shape, size and layout. The city then relaxed several building codes, requirements and fees. Measures waived included mandates for bike parking and open space. And in March 2024, San Francisco voters eliminated a property transfer tax on buildings that were turned into housing, helping to ease some financial burden.

Despite those initiatives, developers remained reluctant to convert properties. Meanwhile, the housing crisis in San Francisco worsened as the expansion of artificial intelligence companies pushed up rents in an already pricey market. In September, the median rent for a one-bedroom apartment in the city was over 25 percent more than it was the prior year and at an all-time high, according to Zumper, a rental platform.

In all, San Francisco’s efforts to make it easier and more financially feasible to convert offices to housing are expected to cut 25 percent off total costs in projects, said Marc Babsin, president of Emerald Fund, a residential development firm in San Francisco. That is a sizable amount even if those reductions, he noted, would be realized only after developers increase property values that go on to generate higher property taxes.

One of the developers trying to take advantage of the tax incentive is Mr. Babsin’s firm, which submitted an application and teamed up with another local developer to buy a midcentury office building. They plan to convert it into 106 apartments. Another developer, Hudson Pacific Properties, a real estate investment trust that owns some 12.5 million square feet of offices and production studios on the West Coast, wants to turn the upper floors of a landmark, 114-year-old building it owns into 136 apartments.

The new tax break “gives developers a way to put together a financing package that can make conversions work,” said Chris Pearson, senior vice president of Hudson Pacific.

The incentives are also playing an important role in the city’s Future of Downtown initiative, a rebuilding program the city’s planning department introduced in 2023.

San Francisco’s office vacancy rate, though improved recently, is among the highest in the country at 30.1 percent, according to Cushman & Wakefield, a commercial real estate brokerage. City officials see more people living downtown as a way to keep the area lively well past 5 p.m. and on weekends. That requires a mix of housing, shops, restaurants and entertainment, said Jacob Bintliff, manager of economic recovery initiatives for the Office of Economic and Workforce Development.

“Everybody feels the pain of where downtown has been since Covid, and there has been a lot of political will to go further with incentives for this category of projects,” he said. “If we were proposing them for some other type of development, maybe we wouldn’t have the same political coalition.”

More of that type of development is needed to give developers confidence to build even bigger, said Steve Luthman, global head of real estate at Hines, a global real estate investor.

The company wants to redevelop a block in the Financial District that could include converting a late-1940s-era office building into housing along with constructing the tallest office skyscraper in the city containing a mix of offices, housing and retail.

But without a broad office conversion effort, the Hines project will remain an island in a district of underused office buildings, Mr. Luthman said.

“The Financial District has always been a single-use district, and every one of our cities in America has one like it,” he said. “So we believe that creating more experiential urban districts is a winning formula, and the leadership shown by a historically anti-development city like San Francisco is giving developers a palate for those projects.”

Even with the new incentives, the advent of A.I. is an unknown in the future of office conversions in San Francisco. Lately, leasing activity and office building values are rising, partly because of the increasing number of A.I. firms looking for space.

More office leasing activity could slow momentum for conversions, as building owners and lenders have become reluctant to part with buildings at a price at which a conversion works financially, Mr. Babsin said. But he is confident that more conversion opportunities will become available.

“There are a lot of A.I. start-ups generating a lot of headlines and a lot of buzz,” Mr. Babsin said. “Nonetheless, dozens of Class B and C office buildings continue to struggle, so we’re bullish on office-to-residential conversions and see an opportunity to bring new energy into downtown.”

item.title: Three Mark Zuckerbergs, Three Surprisingly Different Men
item.description:
By 2010, the year Jesse Eisenberg played the Facebook chief executive Mark Zuckerberg in “The Social Network,” the real Zuckerberg had made only a modest number of public appearances. The first was in 2004, when the 19-year-old executive talked to CNBC about what was then called TheFacebook. In the video he’s composed and articulate, explaining his site’s purpose to an audience that largely wouldn’t have used it, since at the time it was open only to students at select colleges. He maintains direct eye contact. His head moves slightly; his body not at all. His lines sound rehearsed, as if he had practiced a script before this big opening performance.

His body language had barely changed by the time the movie was released six years later. In an interview with Diane Sawyer, his eyes have the same fixed quality. Seated onstage at an advertising conference, his body remains still while he gesticulates with his arms.

The real Zuckerberg’s appearance is a performance from a not particularly gifted actor, though nobody expects a coding genius to be an entertainer. His mannerisms barely shifted as he became more famous. That blankness made it easy for actors to project onto him — Eisenberg, but also Jeremy Strong, who plays him as a seething, embattled middle-aged executive in the new follow-up, “The Social Reckoning.” By now it has become clear just how much of Zuckerberg’s real persona has been an act.

But that was not yet the Zuckerberg we saw in “The Social Network.” As portrayed by Eisenberg, he was a different kind of guy. The general public wasn’t all that familiar with him yet, so Eisenberg didn’t need to do an impression. He had free rein to play the executive as an idea: a smug, insolent teenager secretly desperate for connection.

Thus the Zuckerberg of “The Social Network” is a motormouth, twitchy, brilliant, a brat. He’s a force in perpetual motion, tossing staccato zingers at his opponents and skirting the rules and hierarchies that govern stodgy Harvard. When he comes to rest, it’s to gather energy to strike again. In a scene in which he’s called before a Harvard disciplinary board, his foot taps rapidly, not with nerves so much as pent-up energy, and his eyes dart around the room.

The performance was mesmerizing and netted Eisenberg an Oscar nomination, but it wasn’t much like the real Zuckerberg, who was showing up more and more on TV, still sitting stiffly and only intermittently emoting. After “The Social Network” was released, he told “60 Minutes” that he had liked the movie, but that they had gotten him all wrong.

A month later, Eisenberg hosted “Saturday Night Live” and explained to Andy Samberg — a cast member who’d been impersonating Zuckerberg as a doofy bro — that to play the role, “I speak in short, clipped sentences and I keep my head very still.” (The latter part is debatable.)

In a backstage shot, the real Zuckerberg joked with Lorne Michaels about wanting to join the stars onstage. As he talked, he gestured with his arms in the same way he did in media appearances: bent at a right angle, forearms parallel, cantilevering up and down. Back onstage, Eisenberg continued: “I wasn’t really doing Mark Zuckerberg; I was interpreting a fictional character in a movie script.”

Then the real Zuckerberg walks onstage, ready to play himself. “Jesse, I don’t know if it came off that way,” he says with a practiced smile.

OVER THE YEARS, the possibility of a “Social Network” sequel was floated repeatedly in interviews, and Eisenberg eventually declined to take part in “The Social Reckoning,” the new follow-up. “I don’t want to be associated with that character” anymore, he told Variety.

Instead, Jeremy Strong stepped in. His section of “The Social Reckoning” is set in 2021, just before the release of The Wall Street Journal’s “Facebook Files” investigation. In the conceit of the film, Zuckerberg is preparing, with the aid of lawyers, to testify before Congress. His team is coaching him on the body language required to, as he puts it, appear likable. Nod your head to signal you’re listening. Be nice.

Strong’s Zuckerberg is not Eisenberg’s, and no wonder. We’ve had 16 years of watching Zuckerberg as he grew from wunderkind to chief executive of one of the most powerful, consequential and mistrusted companies in Silicon Valley. We know who this guy is, sort of. He does jiu-jitsu and goes to White House state dinners and makes decisions that affect billions of lives.

Strong’s performance has elements of impersonation. His hair is cropped short and colored a reddish brown. His demeanor is formal and stiff, unlike Eisenberg’s vibrating ball of nerves. He’s sitting at a desk on a stage, with harsh lighting and lines to learn. Strong is a great actor playing a lousy actor who’s preparing for the performance of his life.

But what Strong really nails is Zuckerberg’s eyes. They are unblinking. If Zuckerberg’s expression is generally blank on TV, Strong plays him as though there’s fuming impatience and rage just beneath. Eisenberg’s version was angry, too, but he was jumpy, antsy, annoyed with the sluggishness of the world around him. Strong’s version seems to be filled with molten lava ready to boil over. Even when he’s talking to his employees, he’s frustrated that they’re around at all.

If we were to trace a Zuckerberg arc from Eisenberg to Strong, we’d imagine that the cocky teenager who built a website discovered that when your user base outnumbers the population of whole countries, running a company becomes very difficult. The kid who just wanted to connect became a man who wished everyone would leave him alone. He was never prepared for the consequences of his actions.

But of course, these are fictional versions of Zuckerberg. They’re portrayals of a public figure who dodges efforts to know him.

And that is what’s most interesting about anyone playing the role of Mark Zuckerberg. Unlike some of his colleagues in Silicon Valley, those who ooze charisma and those who seem simply unhinged, Zuckerberg has stage-managed his persona: First he was an awkward genius, then a cool and competent business guy. Lately, he’s played a man’s man, telling the podcaster Joe Rogan that “the corporate world is pretty culturally neutered” and calling for “masculine energy” and “a culture that celebrates the aggression a bit more.” It comes off as a line reading, an echo of something somebody said on the internet.

Who is the real Mark Zuckerberg? It’s hard to say. Eisenberg played him as a type; Strong plays him as the dark side of a guy we know from TV. Zuckerberg himself seems malleable, depending on what’s expedient. Maybe it makes sense that someone who thought we could connect with one another through data-driven profiles and glowing flat screens turns out to be fundamentally unknowable.

item.title: A Contagious Aversion to Overhead Lights
item.description:
Send questions about the office, money, careers and work-life balance to workfriend@nytimes.com. Include your name and location, or a request to remain anonymous. Letters may be edited.

Dear Work Friend,

I manage a team of about 20 people in an open-plan office suite. A few months ago, one of my staff members asked that we disconnect the overhead lighting above his pod because he is prone to migraines. His co-workers didn’t object, so I complied. That corner of the office is now permanently dark, which isn’t ideal, but I’ve been willing to tolerate it.

Last week, a worker in another corner of the office asked to work from home in the morning because her husband’s schedule had changed and she needed to be home to care for her two preschoolers. I said she could change her schedule if necessary, but not work from home while also caring for a 2- and 4-year-old. She escalated to the union, but the union supported my decision.

Yesterday, she came back with a request to have the lights above her desk disconnected as well, saying she also suffers from migraines. Today, a third employee, a close friend of the second, said that she, too, suffers migraines and needs the lights disabled. This feels like a retaliatory protest, and obviously, I cannot agree to the entire office being plunged into a perpetual state of gloom with no overhead lights.

My question is, in declining the two new requests, should I then also revert to full lighting for the whole office? That feels like penalizing a person with a legitimate health need for two disgruntled staffers.

— Anonymous

This is an interesting letter, because I’m not sure the advice you need is the advice you’re looking for.

The answer to your specific question is pretty obvious: No, you should not revert to full lighting for the whole office. Your migraine-suffering employee’s accommodation was made separately from these two later (and, to your mind, suspicious) requests. Right now you have two apparently disgruntled employees; why would you add a third?

I understand why you’re looking to assert some authority here. You’re afraid of being undermined by employee rebellion. (And afraid of a darkened office.) But being a manager isn’t solely about maintaining dispensatory power, and flexibility and creativity can often defuse tension more effectively than a rigid commitment to particular rules — or, for that matter, to particular office lighting schemes.

Rather than roll back accommodations for the sake of fairness (or to make a point), I would at least consider trying to meet your other employees halfway. For all you know, their requests are legitimate and the connection to the contentious schedule change is coincidental. (“Bad migraines” doesn’t seem like a far-fetched condition for a woman with two young kids and a stressful schedule.) Could you, for example, move the two newly incapacitated employees to the same darker section of the office as the original migraine sufferer? This might blunt their frustration, and even earn some good will, without darkening the entire office.

Or you might go in one day this week and try to look at the office lighting as lighting rather than as leverage. Is a less brightly lit office really “gloomy”? Is that one corner “permanently dark,” or naturally — even soothingly — lit? Would individual desk lamps be better for everyone? Is it possible that the migraine sufferers have a point? You could even consult some of the other employees to see how they feel. Some of them may hate the darkness as much as you do, which would at least give you more ground to stand on in rejecting the newer requests.

These exercises may amount to nothing; creativity is not a panacea. And it’s true, you’re backed into a (particularly ill-lit) corner right now because you made the original accommodation informally. But the best alternative to casual flexibility is a formal, neutral and transparent process, not arbitrary rollbacks. In other words, if you can’t absorb tension through creative management, absorb it into bureaucracy.

Your team is big enough and organized enough to run management decisions through the union; why aren’t you also running their accommodation requests through your own process? Ask for medical documentation and discuss alternatives, both for the two new requests and, retroactively, for the original one. If the new requests are bad-faith, you can defensibly shoot them down. And if those two employees can demonstrate need, you’re empowered to help them without feeling undermined.

Dear Work Friend,

A technologist at the laboratory where I work was scheduled to come in at 2 a.m. to relieve the holdover from the second shift. He collided with a deer on his way to work, and his car sustained severe damage. He notified the technologist covering the lab that he’d be returning home rather than risk driving the damaged vehicle any farther.

Because this employee had a history of arriving late to work, the laboratory manager filed an incident report. The technologist went to human resources to plead his case. He was told that in a year’s time the incident would be expunged from his personnel file, but that he needed to address the matter with his manager.

When he went to the manager’s office, he found the manager focused on his computer screen. He tried to hand him the garage’s detailed bill as proof of what had happened, but the manager continued looking at his computer and simply said, “I wouldn’t worry about it.”

This man is well liked around the office, and a group of us wrote a letter on his behalf with the intention of giving it to the C.E.O. He was grateful for what we’d done but, in keeping with his nonconfrontational nature, refused to sign the letter.

Was the laboratory manager justified in maintaining his incident report? Should H.R. have followed up on this matter? And what responsibility, if any, did the manager or H.R. have for what happened to the incident report?

— Anonymous

I agree with your sense that the manager was being unfair in filing the report and that H.R. perhaps should have intervened or declined to escalate the report. I also appreciate the methodical detail with which you recount this story, which probably speaks highly of your skill as a laboratory worker.

But I think the surplus of incidental facts, and your overall sense of frustration with the injustice and unfairness, may be distracting from the practical takeaway of these interactions, which is that most of the people involved seem to want to let the mess die down.

H.R. has said the report will be expunged from his personnel file in a year. The manager has explicitly said not to worry about it. Even the employee in question has declined to join you and your colleagues in your attempt to get the report overturned.

Obviously this doesn’t mean your co-worker is safe from escalation as far as possible escalation goes. And given the manager’s fussy report filing, I understand why you feel concerned.

But your colleague (and you) should be cheered that he has such supportive and well-organized colleagues willing to stand up for him. If the situation develops further — if you get better evidence that the manager or H.R. is truly looking to escalate or retaliate — you already have a protest letter in place. But for now I would listen to H.R., the manager and the technologist themselves and keep it in the drawer.

Dear Work Friend,

I have worked for myself for over 20 years, but the kids are gone, the house is being sold, and I’m contemplating going back to work for someone else. I have some dated experience about what corporate, government and nonprofit workplaces are like.

My question is: What has changed in the past 10 to 20 years that I should take into account as I prepare to do this? As a woman, I expect there to be additional challenges — by most statistics, women over 50 who have not recently been in the work force are not at the top of the hiring list.

There’s lots out there on how to make yourself relevant, how to fill in the gaps in résumés; how #MeToo has had an effect, and a backlash; even how to address ageism. But I don’t get a sense of how the culture itself has changed.

What would you qualify as the biggest workplace cultural changes in the past decade or so? What are things to absolutely avoid, but that might have been acceptable in the past?

Your thoughts are welcome!

— Anonymous

The Lord (and my editors) know that I’m usually all too happy to weigh in on circumstances with which I don’t have a huge amount of personal familiarity. (What kind of advice columnist would I be if I didn’t?)

But given my own demographic categories (a man in his 40s) and work history (checkered), I think any attempt I could make at answering this letter would fall badly flat. Plus, I recently re-entered office work myself, and could use the advice. So it seems like a good opportunity to turn this question over to readers.

What has changed in the workplace? What advice would you give to someone returning to the office from self-employment? What have you had to learn, and what do you wish you’d known?

Send your advice for Anonymous to workfriend@nytimes.com or fill out the form below, and we’ll publish a selection of the letters in a future column.
